retro.headline: Sewer Commission approved added flow for two basement bedrooms and discussed rising FY28 costs and user fees.
retro.summary: The commission approved extra sewer flow for a basement bedroom addition at a single-family home. Staff reviewed the FY27 year-to-date budget, early FY28 planning, pump station aging, and a new discharge permit's cost. The demand fee rate decision and prior minutes were put off until the full board is present, and the public hearing date was left unsettled.

what_happened.line: The Sewer Commission approved additional sewer flow for two added basement bedrooms at a single-family home.
Staff said new discharge permit engineering costs were not budgeted for FY27, and a way was found to pay them this year.
Staff said FY28 lines for capital planning, engineering, electricity and other items are expected to rise, and user fees for FY28 and FY29 need to rise.
Betterment revenue is falling as people pay ahead or sell, leaving user fees as most of revenue.
The sewer demand fee rate decision was put off until the full commission is present; the rate hearing is expected in January.

why_it_matters: Sewer users should expect higher fees in FY28 and FY29, because a falling betterment revenue stream and rising permit, engineering and electricity costs leave user fees to carry more of the system.
The demand fee rate and a public rate hearing are still ahead, so residents on the sewer system will have a chance to weigh in before rates are set.
watch_next: December 8, 6 pm (hybrid): budget discussion meeting.
A public hearing on sewer rates, expected in January; the demand fee rate vote waits for a full commission.

retro.headline: Select Board kept a single tax rate with no exemptions and approved three Verizon conduit petitions.
retro.summary: The board backed a DLTA request to update the housing production plan, approved three Verizon conduit petitions after a public hearing, and held the tax classification hearing, choosing a single rate. The town manager gave her report and a mid-year review of FY27 goals, including FY28 budget planning. The board discussed special town meeting follow-up and went into executive session on the food pantry license.

what_happened.line: After a public hearing, the Select Board voted unanimously to keep a single tax rate, with no open space discount and no residential or small commercial exemption.
The board unanimously approved the Williams Drive, Country Road and Chase Road Verizon conduit petitions as presented.
The board voted unanimously to support a DLTA request for a housing production plan update and authorized the planning director to sign the cover letter.
Special town meeting follow-up ended without a resolution; Brooks House RFP next steps and a TCP decision are to be taken up.
FY28 budget priorities and service levels are tentatively set for December 8th, and the December 1st meeting is cancelled.

why_it_matters: The single-rate vote means homes and businesses stay on the same rate. A split rate was discussed as saving a small amount per home while raising the average business bill by much more.
The FY28 budget discussion and the school committee's first draft, which cites rising costs and restoring four elementary teachers, will shape next year's tax bills and service levels.
watch_next: December 8th: tentative FY28 budget priorities and service-level discussion.
December 3rd: next Select Board meeting, since December 1st is cancelled.

retro.headline: Planning Board approved a bus operations site plan at 199 Mass Ave with six conditions, after a de minimis change.
retro.summary: The board found and approved a de minimis stormwater permit change at 317 Sunny Hill Road, then held a public hearing on a school bus facility at the former car dealership at 199 Mass Ave, closed it and approved with conditions. It also discussed cell tower and battery storage zoning, heard committee reports, approved prior minutes, and adjourned.

what_happened.line: The Planning Board approved the site plan for a school bus facility at 199 Mass Ave, the former car dealership, with six conditions after closing the public hearing.
The conditions cover snow storage, a state driveway permit, lighting, repairs done indoors, operating hours of 6 a.m. to 10 p.m., and parking striped for 60 or more buses.
The board found a stormwater permit change at 317 Sunny Hill Road to be de minimis and approved it.
Cell tower and battery storage zoning were discussed with no vote; the director will send the existing battery storage bylaw to members for comments to town counsel.
Next meetings were set for December 14, January 11 and January 25, with no meeting on December 28.

why_it_matters: The approval lets a school bus operation move into a commercial site on Mass Ave, and the conditions on hours, indoor repairs and parking size set what neighbors can expect there.
Battery storage and cell tower rules are still being drafted, so any zoning change would come later and could reach a Town Meeting vote.
watch_next: Planning Board meeting on December 14, then January 11 and January 25.
Members' comments on the battery storage bylaw, which go to the planning director for town counsel.

retro.headline: Cable committee began planning Comcast license renewal with its lawyer; no votes beyond minutes and adjournment.
retro.summary: The committee reviewed the lawyer's memo and appendices on renewing the Comcast cable license, including falling subscriber numbers and payments, HD channels, capital funding and the school-to-town connection. Once the lawyer joined, he laid out a negotiating strategy, a hearing, an ascertainment document and a capital plan, and assigned tasks. Only the July minutes and adjournment were voted; the next meeting was set for December 14 at 4 p.m.

what_happened.line: The Cable Advisory Committee began planning renewal of the Comcast cable license, working through its lawyer's memo and appendices.
The lawyer set out a negotiating strategy and replaced the departmental survey with a department head meeting and a single public hearing.
The lawyer will model capital funding as a set dollar amount, a percentage or a per-subscriber amount over ten years, and advised listing all needs.
Tasks were assigned: sample documents from the lawyer, information compiled by the manager, and a check on whether the high school connections are live.
Only the July minutes and adjournment were voted; the next meeting was set for December 14 at 4 p.m., likely at the library.

why_it_matters: The Comcast license terms set what the town receives from cable subscribers and what it funds for public, education and government channels, so the renewal affects local channel service and the money behind it.
Franchise payments have fallen as subscribers have declined, so the renewal may rest on capital funding and in-kind terms more than on the 5% fee.
watch_next: Next committee meeting, December 14 at 4 p.m., likely at the library.
The lawyer's sample documents and capital plan models, and the single public hearing on renewal.

retro.headline: Library trustees approved amended October minutes; the food forest grant is still undecided on the governor's desk.
retro.summary: Trustees amended the October minutes, then heard the director's report on the budget, heavy teen room use, and a town-meeting-funded part-time teen librarian. They also heard legal advice on old trust funds, the delayed food forest grant, the director's evaluation timeline, a strategic plan update and a discussion of advocacy. The meeting adjourned by roll call.

what_happened.line: Trustees approved the October minutes as amended, the meeting's only recorded vote besides adjournment.
The director reported on the FY27 operating budget and special revenue balances, including one small grant fund running negative.
Trustees heard that a special town meeting funded a part-time teen room staff librarian position in the FY27 budget revision.
On the food forest grant, trustees heard that the designer's contract did not use prevailing wage, which could raise cost in a worst case.
Trustees set a December 6 return date for evaluation materials and deferred the advocacy plan discussion to January.

why_it_matters: The library's FY27 budget lines for heating, water and sewer, and a funded teen room position bear on what the town budget, mostly taxes, spends on library services this year.
A possible prevailing wage cost on the food forest project could change what that grant-funded work ends up costing.
watch_next: December 6: trustees' evaluation materials are due to the chair, ahead of the December 17 meeting.
January agenda: the deferred advocacy plan discussion.

retro.headline: Cemetery Commission approved updated rules and regulations and set a noon Dec 2 meeting to fund the back-lot expansion.
retro.summary: Bids for the North Cemetery back-lot expansion all came in above expectations, so the commission will meet separately to decide on funding from the sale of lots fund. They reviewed a revised rules and regulations draft, changed wording on plantings and tree planting, and moved to approve it. They also discussed the West Street Terrace easement and the pricing rollout.

what_happened.line: The Cemetery Commission set a short meeting for noon on Wednesday, December 2, to discuss and vote on paying for the back-lot expansion from the sale of lots fund.
All nine bids for the North Cemetery back-lot expansion came in higher than expected, and money left in the capital project would not cover the low bid.
The commission reviewed a revised rules and regulations draft, changed the planting and tree-planting wording, and moved to approve it; the vote was not audible.
The December 17 meeting was cancelled, and the January meeting is to be decided later, likely by Zoom.
Before pursuing the West Street Terrace easement, the commission will talk to the attorney, surveyor and landowner and assign costs.

why_it_matters: The expansion would add burial space at North Cemetery, and the commission is looking at the sale of lots fund, which is lot-sale money rather than the general tax levy, to cover the gap left by high bids.
The new rules and regulations set how plantings and trees are handled on cemetery lots, so they affect families who visit or maintain graves.
watch_next: Special Cemetery Commission meeting at noon on Wednesday, December 2, with a vote on funding the back-lot expansion from the sale of lots fund.
The recorded vote on the rules and regulations, which was not audible in the recording.

retro.headline: Capital committee heard fire and police capital plans and questioned a third ambulance; only adjournment was voted.
retro.summary: After a member raised a Town Meeting complaint that capital procedures are unfair to the schools, the committee heard the new fire chief's ten-year plan and the police chief's vehicle and equipment plan. Discussion centred on adding a third ambulance, moving tasers into the operating budget, and the special vehicle stabilization fund. No substantive votes were taken.

what_happened.line: The Capital Planning Committee heard the fire and police capital plans and took no votes other than adjournment.
The fire chief's ten-year plan drew discussion of adding a third ambulance as a mechanical spare, with a member arguing it must be justified by billing revenue.
Members and the chief suggested the special vehicle stabilization fund might cover the rescue pumper and the ambulance.
On police items, members favoured putting tasers in the operating budget rather than a multi-year payment plan, and the chief expects FY27 cruisers to come in under the approved number.
A member raised a complaint that capital procedures are unfair to the schools; it would become a future agenda item if taken up.

why_it_matters: Ambulances, fire trucks, cruisers and equipment are paid through the capital plan, so choices about the stabilization fund, the operating budget or grants affect what appears on future Town Meeting warrants and tax bills.
Moving tasers into the operating budget would shift a recurring cost from the capital plan to the yearly operating budget, which is mostly paid by taxes.
watch_next: Nov 30 at 6:30: the committee meets on DPW and IT capital requests.
Dec 7 at 6:30: the committee meets on school and facilities department requests.

retro.headline: Committee heard a first-draft FY28 budget up about 10.77%, took no vote, and voted to send a Collins Center study to FinCom.
retro.summary: The committee approved three line-item transfers and heard a version-one FY28 budget that includes all staff requests, with no action on its total. Members debated how far to rethink programs, including MassCore, Monty Tech and transportation. They also appointed a MASC delegate, voted to take a Collins Center efficiency study proposal to the Finance Committee, and went into executive session on an open meeting law complaint.

what_happened.line: The School Committee heard a first-draft FY28 budget that includes all staff requests, and took no vote on its total.
The committee voted 4-0 to ask the Finance Committee to pay for a Collins Center efficiency study.
The committee approved three line-item transfers, 4-0, including money from an unfilled psychologist position moved to contracted services.
Members discussed rising health insurance, transportation and electricity costs, and the cost of the Monty Tech assessment against in-house vocational classes.
The committee unanimously appointed a MASC delegate, then went into executive session on an open meeting law complaint.

why_it_matters: The FY28 school budget is the largest piece of the town budget, mostly paid by taxes, and this first version lists every staff request before any cuts or offsets are chosen.
The Collins Center study, if the Finance Committee funds it from its reserve fund, could shape which programs and services are changed in later versions of the budget.
watch_next: The Finance Committee's response to the request to pay for the Collins Center study from its reserve fund.
Later versions of the FY28 budget, and the monthly FY27 and FY28 budget updates planned once the new business manager starts.

retro.headline: Water commissioners set special meeting articles, with not-to-exceed caps, and agreed a $500 staff bonus.
retro.summary: Commissioners reviewed Meadow Lane/Rolling Acres water main costs done in-house and moved a bonus for staff. They put off the Tighe & Bond blending proposal for two weeks of review, then worked through the special meeting articles (National Grid bill, well cleaning, well testing, engineering) and approved them with not-to-exceed wording. A long discussion covered PFAS blending targets, DEP, and tank maintenance.

what_happened.line: Water commissioners approved the special meeting articles as written, with articles two, three and four amended to read "not to exceed" the stated amounts.
Article three, for well testing and exploration, was raised to cover a hydrogeologist study and an area review; the other articles' amounts were left unchanged.
Commissioners deferred the Tighe & Bond blending evaluation proposal for about two weeks of review.
A motion to give each staff member who worked on the Meadow Lane / Rolling Acres water main a bonus was made; the outcome is not audible in the recording.
A plan for tank inspection and maintenance was deferred, with the annual meeting as the aim.

why_it_matters: The special meeting articles move money from the district's surplus toward well cleaning, well testing and engineering, so residents who vote on them will be deciding how that surplus is spent.
The not-to-exceed wording sets a ceiling on each transfer, and the deferred blending proposal bears on how the district meets PFAS treatment targets and what that costs water customers.
watch_next: The next commissioners' meeting in early December, which is to ready the motions for the special meeting.
The revised Tighe & Bond blending proposal, due back for review in about two weeks.

retro.headline: Assessors voted to recommend a single tax rate and no residential exemption, small commercial exemption or open space discount.
retro.summary: The board approved prior minutes and rehearsed its FY2027 tax classification presentation for the Select Board, suggesting edits to slides and charts. With one member gone, two members voted recommendations on the four classification options. They also discussed the veterans exemption article for May town meeting, upcoming meeting dates, and the unfilled data collector position.

what_happened.line: Two assessors voted to recommend a single tax rate instead of a split rate for FY2027, to be presented to the Select Board.
The board also voted to recommend no open space discount, no residential exemption and no small commercial exemption.
The board heard that a split rate would save the average home a small amount while commercial, industrial and personal property would pay much more.
The veterans exemption cost-of-living and doubling article was postponed to May town meeting, for implementation in 2028, with impact statements to be prepared.
The December 16 meeting is held in abeyance. The next meeting is December 2, with January 6 tentative.

why_it_matters: The classification choice decides how the property tax levy is divided between homeowners and commercial, industrial and personal property owners. It shapes the tax rate on every bill.
The veterans exemption article is expected at May town meeting, where residents will be asked to vote on it. The change would not take effect until 2028.
watch_next: The Select Board's tax classification decision on the assessors' recommendations.
The next Board of Assessors meeting on December 2, with January 6 tentative.

retro.headline: Town Meeting approved $195,830 from general stabilization for track and field engineering, 57-18, after striking the payback paragraph.
retro.summary: The special town meeting heard a Brooks House report and passed a budget amendment, an old-bill payment and two bylaw amendments. Voters gave advisory support for demolishing the TC Passios building and for a stormwater enterprise fund. The final article funded design engineering for the middle school track and field from stabilization.

what_happened.line: Town Meeting approved a transfer from the general stabilization fund to pay for professional engineering of the middle school track and fields, after striking the payback paragraph.
Voters struck the second paragraph of article 9, which stated an intent to repay the stabilization fund from free cash.
In non-binding votes, the meeting favored pursuing demolition of the TC Passios building and favored a stormwater utility fee over funding stormwater from the operating budget.
The meeting passed an omnibus budget amendment with a WRAP fund transfer, and a transfer from the FY2027 school line to pay a prior-year bill.
The meeting passed over the special education reserve article, with no certified free cash and no funding policy, and passed two bylaw amendments on zoning and stormwater fees.

why_it_matters: Stabilization is the town's savings, so spending it on track engineering leaves less cushion, and a larger construction cost still has no stated funding source, which would likely mean borrowing paid from the operating budget and taxes.
The stormwater advisory vote points toward a flat annual utility fee on homes, with bills starting in July 2028 if adopted, and it would still need a binding vote.
watch_next: School committee and finance committee agreed to revisit the special education reserve fund in spring.
Binding action on the TC Passios demolition and a stormwater utility, since both votes were advisory only.

retro.headline: School Committee voted 4-0 to back Article 9 track and field engineering, funded from general stabilization.
retro.summary: A special remote meeting was held because FY26 free cash is not closed out or certified, leaving no funding source for Article 9 at the next night's special town meeting. After public comment, the committee voted to keep the article and name the general stabilization fund as the source, intending to replenish it from free cash later. what_happened.line: The School Committee voted 4-0 to keep Article 9, track and field engineering, in the warrant and to name the general stabilization fund as its funding source.
The vote came at a special remote meeting because FY26 free cash is not closed out or certified, so none is available for the special town meeting.
The vote says the stabilization money is to be replaced once free cash is available.
The committee agreed to affirm its intent to bring a spring warrant article replacing the stabilization money with free cash, noting it cannot bind town meeting.
Two public comments followed: one urged naming stabilization as the source, and one urged a well-planned long-term track and field project.

why_it_matters: Article 9 would draw on reserve savings, not free cash, so residents at town meeting are asked to approve a transfer that needs a two-thirds vote and leaves the reserve lower until it is replaced.
Whether the reserve is refilled depends on a separate spring town meeting vote, which the committee cannot guarantee.
watch_next: The special town meeting the night after this meeting, where Article 9 needs a two-thirds vote.
The spring warrant article to replace the stabilization money with free cash, once FY26 free cash is certified.

retro.headline: Committee moved to oppose a separate stormwater utility and to ask the state delegation to help with a liquor license.

what_happened.line: The Economic Development Committee took up a motion not to support a separate stormwater utility; the minutes record it moved and seconded, but the vote was not audible.

A motion to reach out to the state delegation about the liquor license process was made and seconded; the outcome was not audible, and a member will email the delegation.

watch_next: The member's email to the state delegation about the liquor license process.
A recurring meeting date, to be set after the town schedule is checked.

retro.headline: Sewer commission approved the Q2 FY27 commitment and aimed to hold a January 12 hearing on late fees.
retro.summary: The commission heard about an irrigation deduct meter billing error caused by wrong reading dates from the water department and a billing system rate setting, since corrected. It was told the CTE contract bid was postponed and the current contract extended three months, reviewed Fitchburg and Leominster flow capacity, and discussed the sewer demand fee and interest rate. It voted the quarterly commitment and agreed to take up the budget line by line, including preventive maintenance, on December 8.

what_happened.line: The Sewer Commission voted, 3 in favor on a roll call, to approve the Q2 fiscal year 27 sewer commitment.
The commission plans a public hearing on sewer rates and the demand fee for January 12, with firm numbers to be set at the next meeting.
Staff compared late fees and interest in surrounding towns; the commission leans toward a modest increase below the state maximum.
The commission heard that wrong reading dates from the water department gave some customers too large an irrigation meter deduct in Q1; bills were corrected and remailed.
The CTE contract was extended three months at the existing rate while the bid is re-posted.

why_it_matters: Sewer bills may rise through a higher demand fee or late-interest rate, and residents can speak at the planned January hearing before those rates are set.
Residents with irrigation deduct meters should check that their corrected Q1 and Q2 bills match their meter readings.
The budget, including whether money is set aside for preventive maintenance after an emergency pump replacement, is still open and will shape future sewer costs.
watch_next: December 8 meeting: line-by-line budget discussion, including preventive maintenance.
January 12: planned public hearing on sewer rates and the demand fee, with firm numbers to be set at the next meeting.

retro.headline: Planning Board endorsed five ANR plans and approved a shared-driveway special permit at 760 Goodrich Street.
retro.summary: The board endorsed ANR plans for five properties, then held a hearing on a shared driveway at 760 Goodrich Street. It approved the special permit with a homeowners association condition and accepted a de minimis stormwater change. It also extended a stormwater bond for 100 Townsend Harbor Road, heard committee reports and approved minutes.

what_happened.line: The Planning Board approved a special permit for a shared driveway at 760 Goodrich Street, with a homeowners association condition before occupancy permits.
The board found a stormwater alteration at 760 Goodrich de minimis and accepted the change.
The board endorsed ANR plans for five properties, including Howard Street, Leominster Road, Sunny Hill Road, Mass Ave and Northfield Road.
The board extended the stormwater bond for 100 Townsend Harbor Road through July 1, 2028, after the builder asked for more time.
The director will write the 760 Goodrich decision for members, with signing to follow if no changes come by next Monday.

why_it_matters: The Goodrich Street permit sets a homeowners association condition on a shared driveway, which decides who is responsible for it once homes are occupied.
The bond extension at Townsend Harbor Road keeps stormwater security in place for five lots while construction runs longer, which protects the town from paying for unfinished drainage work.
watch_next: Signing of the 760 Goodrich Street decision, expected after next Monday if members request no changes.
Next Planning Board meetings on November 23, December 14 and January 11 and 25; none on December 28.
